sweep_summary: Three works with stress in the title for Beja (catalog: 'conflict', Almkvist 1881 weight-based vs Wedekind et al. 2008 lexical/morphemic pitch accent). Strunk 1961 is a Glottolog mis-attachment (Mycenaean Greek orthography; De Gruyter DOI; irrelevant). Vanhove 2008 (Peeters volume, HAL notice only, no file) is about intonation of converb clauses per its FR/EN abstracts, not word stress; low priority. Hudson 1973 'Syllables, moras and accents in Beja' was downloaded in full from the author's own site (dickhudson.com; DOI 10.1017/S0022226700003534 paywalled at CUP) and read: pitch accent system, 'the position of the accent is unpredictable', accent located 0 or 1 place (syllable, else mora) before a fixed point = last mora of the stem, the choice being lexical/grammatical, plural marked by a one-place shift; no syllable-weight placement rule. The same page yielded Hudson 1974 'A structural sketch of Beja' (African Language Studies 15), whose §1.4 states outright that accent 'is not predictable (pace Reinisch, 1893: 55 and Almkvist, 1881: 57) from its purely phonological structure' and is set by inherent final/penultimate morpheme accents within accent-units. Both files with and lines. Bearing on the catalog: refines, not resolves -- Hudson is the best first-hand statement for the lexical/morphological pole and should be added to the record (stronger than Wedekind 2008 for that side), but the weight-based readings (Almkvist, Reinisch, Vanhove 2020 §1.2) remain in the literature, so the 'conflict' code stands pending Vanhove 2017 'Le bedja' or the LangSci 603 sketch. all look-ups were done through Crossref/HAL APIs and direct downloads.

new_statements.quote: The position and nature of the realized accent is determined by the word's morphological structure, and is not predictable (pace Reinisch, 1893: 55 and Almkvist, 1881 : 57) from its purely phonological structure (e.g. /ti-rib-'a/ ' you refused ', but /ti-dif-a/ you went', whose roots belong to different accentual classes but are otherwise morphologically the same). A morpheme may or may not have an inherent accent, but if it does, there are two further variables to be specified : the position of the accentual reference-point (usually on a vowel in the last syllable of the morpheme) and the position of the accented vowel relative to this reference-point
new_statements.citation: Hudson, R. A. (1974). A structural sketch of Beja. African Language Studies 15: 111-142, §1.4 'Accent' (with Hudson, R. A. 1973, Syllables, moras and accents in Beja, Journal of Linguistics 9: 53-63, as the fuller analysis)
new_statements.reading: First-hand modern description (Hudson's own fieldwork, Port Sudan/Tokar varieties per Vanhove 2006): Beja word accent is a pitch accent whose placement is lexical-morphological, not weight-driven. Each accented morpheme carries an inherent accent of one of two types, 'final' (on its reference-point, normally the last vowel of the morpheme) or 'penultimate' (one syllable, or failing that one mora, before it); in a polymorphemic accent-unit the later inherent accent wins; plural formation typically swaps final for penultimate accent. Hudson 1973 adds that placement is counted in syllables where the accent-unit allows and in moras otherwise, that long vowels are bimoraic (level vs falling pitch), and states flatly that 'the position of the accent is unpredictable'. This is the strongest source for the lexical/morphological pole of the catalog's recorded conflict and explicitly argues against the quantity-based rules of Almkvist and Reinisch; it aligns with Wedekind et al. 2008 and Vanhove 2014 §2.4, against Vanhove 2020 §1.2. The 'conflict' code therefore stands, but Hudson 1973/1974 should be cited in the record as the primary first-hand statement for the non-weight side (it predates and is more analytically explicit than Wedekind 2008).

new_statements.quote: In words used in isolation, stress assignment rules are mostly, but not always, conditioned by their syllabic structure, and may vary with the presence of certain affixes and clitics. It does not go further left than the ante-penultimate syllable, except for certain persons in the Prohibitive (see Section 7.3.2.2.10). [...] In verbs, stress falls either on the stem or the inflectional morpheme, depending on the verb class and on TAM [...] Stress assignment of nouns and adjectives depends on their syllabic structure to a large extent, but not without exceptions. [...] Beja has two tones, H and L, which are marginal and only occur in nouns and adjectives on syllables with long vowels.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Citation-form word stress (central/Sinkat and southern Sudanese Beja) is described as MOSTLY conditioned by syllabic structure within a three-syllable window (never left of the antepenult), with a morphological component and lexical residue: (a) verbs: stress on stem vs inflectional affix according to verb class (V1 prefixing / V2 suffixing), person and TAM; imperative stress position distinguishes V1 from V2; (b) nouns/adjectives, singular: disyllables with a long vowel in a closed final syllable -> final stress (kiˈtaːb); disyllables with a long first vowel -> initial (ˈkoːlaj); CaCi, CiCi, CaCCi, CiCa, CHaCa, CVCCa and Ci/aCiC shapes -> final; CaCa, CVːC(C)i, CHiCa/i, HaCCi -> initial; reduplicated stems -> penultimate; tri- and quadrisyllables -> usually penultimate; C(H)a/iCaC disyllables -> 'unpredictable and lexically assigned' (ˈgalam vs baˈlad); (c) stress moves when articles, stressed clitic pronouns, postpositions or plural -(j)a are added (ˈragad / raˈgad-a; tiˈrig / ˈuː=trig); (d) two marginal tones H/L only on long vowels of nouns/adjectives, analysed after Hudson 1973 as stress on the 2nd vs 1st mora, used for sg/pl of indefinite vowel-final nouns (ʃʔáː=b 'a cow' / pl. ʃʔàː=b) and for emphasis; stress alone distinguishes only three known minimal pairs. In connected speech stress 'heavily depends on pragmatics, speech tempo and intonation contours and still needs to be studied'. §7.1 states the sketch revises Vanhove 2014/2017a precisely on 'vowels, stress, tones'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress described (0 hits for 'secondary stress'); the affirmative optative is said to carry two stresses (on the particle bi= and on the verb stem, Table 7.24), the negative optative 'only one stress on the stem'.
new_statements.exceptions: heːˈkʷal 'lucky' (final despite long first vowel); baˈwa 'shelter' (final despite CaCa); Arabic loan ˈkoːfijaːj 'beany' antepenultimate (trisyllables otherwise penultimate) with stress shift in pl. koːˈfi-jij; C(H)a/iCaC nouns lexically split; Prohibitive particle ˈbaː=/ˈbiː= is 'the sole exception to the rule that stress assignment does not go further to the antepenultimate syllable' (fn.6 p.801); some verb clitics stressed (=eːk 'if'); suːg 'market' sg L tone / pl H tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Vanhove 2017 describes the Sinkat variety (central Beja, Sudan) with comparisons to northern and southern varieties (the Harvard library catalogue description); Vanhove & Hamid Ahmed 2026 is a Sudan Beja dictionary with sketch; Vanhove 2008 uses her Sudan (Sinkat area) corpus.

tone_statements.citation: Wedekind, Klaus (2004). Beja phonology: an update. Folia Orientalia 40. pp. 71-91.
tone_statements.quote: The suprasegmentals are (1) pitch-accent and (2) length - i.e. vowel length and consonant gemination. There also are the intonational pitch movements which characterize non-tonal languages. Like other Cushitic languages, Beja need not be analyzed as a tone language. The analysis in terms of pitch-accent seems preferable both for reasons of economy and adequacy … As an inherent lexical property, every Beja morpheme has its proper "pitch-accent" placement. … this particular syllable is "louder" and of "higher pitch" than the other(s). … Beja is not a "stress" language.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 76-77, section 'Suprasegmentals: pitch accent and length (gemination)' / 'pitch accent and intonation'
tone_statements.summary: Not analysed as a tone language: lexical pitch accent, at least one accented (louder, higher-pitched) syllable per morpheme, shifted by affixes and in plurals; intonation as in non-tonal languages.

tone_statements.citation: Wedekind, Klaus and Wedekind, Charlotte and Musa, Abuzeinab (2008). Beja pedagogical grammar: online monograph. Afrikanistik online.
tone_statements.quote: Every Beja word will have at least one syllable which is louder and which has a higher pitch than the other(s). The louder syllable is said to carry the pitch-accent (or accent for short). In this book the accent is transcribed with bold letters. [par. 27] ... Briefly, the main rules concerning pitch-accent (accent for short) are as follows: 1. Every morpheme or word root has its inherent accent. The accent is part of the root - in the same way as the meaning, the gender, or the consonants and vowels are parts of it. 2. If a word consists of several morphemes, (only) the last accent will be articulated. 3. Plurals will shift the accent toward the beginning of the word by one syllable (This rule does not apply in the Bishaari dialect). [par. 45]

readall_conflicts: Hudson 1976 (p. 97) restates, against Almkvist 1881 and Reinisch 1893, that Beja word accents follow regular (morphological) patterns and may be treated as a kind of tone system, which sides with the existing Hudson 1973/1974 statement (pitch accent, morpheme-inherent final vs penultimate accent, not weight-driven) and with Vanhove 2014 §2.4 (stress not conditioned by syllable structure; lexically assigned in nouns, category- and affix-dependent in verbs). The catalog's recorded conflict is between that lexical-morphological pole and the quantity-based rules of Almkvist/Reinisch (and Vanhove 2020 §1.2 per the existing statement); nothing opened here resolves it, because Hudson 1976 §2.4 itself, Vanhove 2017 and the forthcoming Vanhove & Hamid-Ahmed sketch are not open. Vanhove 2008 and Salt 1814 are silent.

If a word consists of several morphemes, (only) the last accent will be articulated. 3. Plurals will shift the accent toward the beginning of the word by one syllable (This rule does not apply in the Bishaari dialect). [par. 45]

tone.quote: The suprasegmentals are (1) pitch-accent and (2) length - i.e. vowel length and consonant gemination. There also are the intonational pitch movements which characterize non-tonal languages. Like other Cushitic languages, Beja need not be analyzed as a tone language. The analysis in terms of pitch-accent seems preferable both for reasons of economy and adequacy … As an inherent lexical property, every Beja morpheme has its proper "pitch-accent" placement. … this particular syllable is "louder" and of "higher pitch" than the other(s). … Beja is not a "stress" language.
tone.locator: pp. 76-77, section 'Suprasegmentals: pitch accent and length (gemination)' / 'pitch accent and intonation'
tone.summary: Not analysed as a tone language: lexical pitch accent, at least one accented (louder, higher-pitched) syllable per morpheme, shifted by affixes and in plurals; intonation as in non-tonal languages.
tone.says: Not analysed as a tone language: lexical pitch accent, at least one accented (louder, higher-pitched) syllable per morpheme, shifted by affixes and in plurals; intonation as in non-tonal languages.
